steps.say: Hello, explorer! This is our Earth, right now. Each dot is an earthquake from this week. An earthquake is when the ground shakes.
Look at the giant ocean in the middle. It is the Pacific Ocean. See all the dots around its edges? People call it the Ring of Fire.
The outside of the Earth is cracked into giant pieces, like a cracked eggshell. The ground shakes where the pieces push and slide past each other.
This was the biggest earthquake this week, near {quake.place}.

If the ground ever shakes where you are: Drop, Cover, and Hold On! Get down on your hands and knees, cover your head and neck, crawl under a strong table if one is close, and hold on until the shaking stops.

quiz.q: An earthquake is when the ground shakes.
quiz.why: Yes! The ground shakes when big pieces of rock under it suddenly move.

quiz.q: Where do lots of earthquakes happen?
a: Around the edges of the Pacific Ocean
quiz.why: Most big earthquakes happen around the Pacific Ocean, the Ring of Fire.

quiz.q: Tap the safety steps in the right order.
quiz.why: Drop down, cover your head, and hold on until the shaking stops.

steps.say: These dots are this week's earthquakes, from the U.S. Geological Survey. Bigger dots are bigger earthquakes. Notice they don't fall just anywhere: they make lines.
Earth's hard outer shell is broken into huge pieces called plates. They move very slowly, a few centimetres a year. Where plates meet, rock gets stuck, then slips. That slip is an earthquake.
The lines of dots trace the edges of the plates. Around the Pacific, the edges make a loop people call the Ring of Fire. It has volcanoes too.
Scientists rate an earthquake's size with a number called magnitude. Each step up the scale means far more energy: a magnitude 6 releases about 32 times as much energy as a magnitude 5.
Here is this week's biggest earthquake: magnitude {quake.mag}, near {quake.place}.

quiz.q: What causes most earthquakes?
a: Plates of Earth's outer shell slipping past each other
quiz.why: Most earthquakes happen when rock on a fault suddenly slips, mostly along plate edges.

quiz.q: About how many of the world's biggest earthquakes happen around the Pacific Ring of Fire?
quiz.why: The USGS says about 81 percent of the largest earthquakes happen in the belt around the Pacific.

quiz.q: A magnitude 6 earthquake releases about the same energy as a magnitude 5.
quiz.why: No. Each whole step up releases about 32 times more energy.

quiz.q: Tap these from weakest to strongest.
quiz.why: Bigger magnitude numbers mean much stronger earthquakes.

g68.title: Plates, depth and the Ring of Fire

steps.say: This week's earthquakes from the USGS. They outline the edges of Earth's tectonic plates, the rigid pieces of the lithosphere that move a few centimetres a year.
Now we can see through the Earth. Each quake is drawn at its real depth, stretched 25 times so you can see it. Most are shallow, but some are hundreds of kilometres down.
Deep earthquakes happen where one plate sinks beneath another, called subduction. Follow the dots: they get deeper as you move away from the ocean trench, tracing the sinking slab.
This week's biggest: magnitude {quake.mag}, {quake.depth} km deep, near {quake.place}.
Magnitude measures the size of the earthquake at its source. One whole step up means about 32 times more energy, so two steps is about 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000 times.

quiz.q: Where do most very deep earthquakes happen?
a: Where one plate sinks beneath another (subduction zones)
Where plates pull apart in the middle of oceans
Under the middle of continents, far from any plate edge
quiz.why: Deep earthquakes occur within plates sinking into the mantle at subduction zones.
src: USGS: Determining the depth of an earthquake

quiz.q: Each whole step up in magnitude releases about how many times more energy?
quiz.why: About 32 times per whole step; two steps is 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000 times.

quiz.q: Scientists can predict the day and place of the next big earthquake.
quiz.why: No scientist has ever predicted a major earthquake. Scientists calculate the probability of one in an area over many years instead.

src: USGS: Determining the depth of an earthquake

steps.say: This week's earthquakes from the USGS feed. Before reading patterns into a map, ask what it can and can't see.

Notice the many small quakes in the western U.S. and Alaska. That is partly because dense seismic networks there catch small quakes that go unrecorded in much of the world. Small dots here reflect detection, not only shaking.
Seen through the Earth, depth tells the story of each boundary: shallow quakes along ridges and transform faults, deep ones only in sinking slabs.
Magnitude is the size at the source; damage depends on depth, distance, ground and buildings. A deep magnitude 7 can do less harm than a shallow 6 near a city.
This week's largest: magnitude {quake.mag} near {quake.place}, {quake.hrs} hours before the data was collected.

quiz.q: Why does the map show many small earthquakes in the U.S. but few elsewhere?
a: Denser seismic networks there detect smaller quakes
The U.S. has more earthquakes than Japan or Indonesia
Other countries' quakes are hidden on purpose
quiz.why: Earthquake catalogues grow with the number of seismic instruments: more instruments record more small quakes. Coverage is densest in parts of the U.S.
src: USGS: Why are we having so many earthquakes?

quiz.q: What does magnitude measure?
a: The size of the earthquake at its source
How far away people felt it
quiz.why: Magnitude is the size at the source, and each step means about 32 times more energy; shaking and damage at a place are described by intensity.

quiz.q: A magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times the energy of a magnitude 5.
Scientists can predict the day and place of the next big earthquake.
quiz.why: No; forecasts are probabilities over years.

goals: Most volcanoes and earthquakes mark the edges of tectonic plates; the Ring of Fire around the Pacific is the most active zone in the world.
Plates meet at three main kinds of boundary: divergent (moving apart, like Iceland), convergent (moving together, often one plate sinking under another), and transform (sliding past each other).
Some volcanoes, like Hawaii's, form far from any plate edge over a hotspot, and the weekly volcano report lists only volcanoes with notable activity that week.

Why might a volcano that has been erupting for years not show up in this week's volcano report?
Earthquakes along the San Andreas Fault are shallow, but some under the western Pacific are hundreds of kilometres deep. What is different about those two places?

g35.title: The Ring of Fire and other volcano homes

steps.say: These are the volcanoes in this week's Smithsonian / USGS volcano report. Look at the Pacific Ocean: notice how many sit around its edges.
Now add this week's earthquakes. Volcanoes and earthquakes line up along the same belts. These belts are the edges of the giant moving pieces of Earth's outer shell, called plates.
Around the Pacific, the Pacific Plate meets many other plates. Scientists call this the Ring of Fire: the most active zone for earthquakes and volcanoes in the world.
Iceland sits right on top of a crack where two plates are pulling apart. Melted rock rises into the gap, so Iceland has many volcanoes. Melted rock underground is called magma.
Hawaii is different: it is more than 3,200 km from the nearest plate edge. Its volcanoes grow over a very hot spot deep under the plate.
This week's report lists {volc.n} volcanoes ({volc.week}). Tap a triangle to read what the scientists wrote about it.

quiz.q: Why do volcanoes and earthquakes line up in long belts?
a: They mark the edges of Earth's plates
They happen where it rains most
quiz.why: Earthquakes and volcanoes mark the boundaries between moving plates.
src: Smithsonian GVP: This Dynamic Planet map

quiz.q: In Iceland, two plates are pulling apart.
quiz.why: Iceland is splitting along the spreading line between the North American and Eurasian Plates.

quiz.q: About how far is Hawaii from the nearest plate edge?
quiz.why: Hawaii formed in the middle of the Pacific, more than 3,200 km from the nearest plate boundary.

quiz.q: Magma is melted rock that forms deep inside the Earth.
quiz.why: Magma is molten rock formed deep within the Earth. Once it erupts, it is called lava.

steps.say: Volcanoes from this week's report and the latest earthquakes. Notice how they trace lines across the globe. Those lines are plate boundaries.
Boundary type 1, divergent: plates move apart and new crust forms. Iceland straddles the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian Plates spread about 2.5 cm a year.

Boundary type 2, convergent: plates move toward each other and one can sink under the other. This is subduction. It makes deep ocean trenches, like the Mariana Trench here, and feeds volcanoes like those in the Andes and the Cascades.
Turn on x-ray to see quakes at their real depth. Under the subduction zones, notice quakes going down into the Earth along the sinking plate: the deepest reach about 700 km.
Boundary type 3, transform: plates slide past each other sideways, like the San Andreas Fault in California. These quakes are shallow, and there are few volcanoes.
And Hawaii, far from any boundary, sits over a hotspot. This week's report: {volc.n} volcanoes, {volc.week}. Which boundary type is each one near?

quiz.q: At which kind of boundary do plates move apart?
quiz.why: Divergent boundaries are spreading centres where plates move apart and new crust forms.

quiz.q: Where do the deepest earthquakes happen?
a: Inside plates sinking at subduction zones
Along transform faults like the San Andreas
quiz.why: The deepest quakes, to about 700 km, happen inside subducting slabs. Transform faults are active only to about 20 km.
src: USGS: At what depth do earthquakes occur?

quiz.q: Kauai is far northwest of the hotspot; the Big Island sits over it. Which has older rocks?
quiz.why: Kauai's oldest rocks are about 5.5 million years old; the Big Island's oldest exposed rocks are less than 0.7 million years old. The Pacific Plate carries islands away from the hotspot.

quiz.q: Ocean trenches, the deepest parts of the ocean floor, are created by subduction.
quiz.why: Trenches form where one plate dives under another. The Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is nearly 11,000 m deep.

steps.say: Volcanoes from the Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report, with recent USGS earthquakes. The Ring of Fire, where the Pacific Plate meets many surrounding plates, is the most seismically and volcanically active zone in the world.

This week's report covers {volc.week} and lists {volc.n} volcanoes. Notice that is far fewer than the roughly 1,350 potentially active volcanoes worldwide. The report is not a census of everything erupting.

GVP says the report does not necessarily include all volcanic activity that week. A volcano is typically included when an alert level changes, an ash advisory is issued, or a credible report describes new or changed activity. The report has two parts, New Activity/Unrest and Continuing Activity. Routine activity at the dozen or so volcanoes that have erupted almost nonstop for decades is typically not reported, and seafloor volcanism seldom is.
It is also compiled fast, with little time for fact-checking, so items may later prove wrong. Treat each entry as a pointer to the observatory's own reports, not the final word.
Depth tells the boundary story. With x-ray on, quakes under subduction zones reach about 700 km inside the sinking slab, while transform faults stay shallow, to about 20 km.

Divergent, convergent, transform: Iceland splits along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between the North American and Eurasian Plates. Hawaii, over 3,200 km from any boundary, is classically explained by a hotspot, though USGS authors note hotspots may be neither deep nor fixed. Science still argues about it.

quiz.q: The Weekly Volcanic Activity Report lists every volcano that erupted that week.
quiz.why: It summarizes activity that meets set criteria. Routine activity at volcanoes that have erupted almost continuously for decades is typically not reported, and seafloor volcanism is seldom reported.
src: Smithsonian / USGS Weekly Volcanic Activity Report

goals: The Earth has layers: a thin rigid crust, about 2,900 km of hot, slowly flowing mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core of iron and nickel.
No one has ever drilled below about 12 km. What we know of the deep Earth comes mainly from earthquake waves: P waves cross solids and liquids, S waves cannot cross liquid.

Reference models such as PREM, IASP91 and ak135 are fitted to seismic travel times. They agree on the big picture and differ by kilometres on the details; some questions (the innermost inner core, how the inner core turns) are still debated.
discuss: If S waves cannot travel through liquid, what would seismometers on the far side of the Earth record after a big earthquake? What would that tell you?
The crust is about 5 km thick under the oceans and about 30 km under continents. Why might thin, young ocean crust be where new plate is made?
Three reference models put the core-mantle boundary at 2,889, 2,891 and 2,891.5 km. Is that disagreement a problem, or a sign of how well the boundary is known?

steps.say: Look at our planet. We live on the very outside of it.
The Earth has layers inside, a bit like a boiled egg.
The outside layer is the crust. It is thin, like an eggshell. We live on the crust.
Under the crust is the mantle. It is very hot rock that moves very, very slowly.
In the middle is the core. It is mostly metal: iron and nickel.
Nobody can dig that deep. Scientists listen to earthquake waves to learn what is inside. Look at the layers here.

steps.say: These are this week's earthquakes. Each one sends waves through the inside of the Earth, and instruments all over the world record them.
The biggest one this week was magnitude {quake.mag}, {quake.place}. It started {quake.depth} km underground.
Even the deepest hole ever drilled reaches only about 12 km. To learn what is deeper, scientists study how earthquake waves travel.
The crust is thin: about 5 km under the oceans and about 30 km under the continents, on average.
Turn on x-ray to see quakes at their real depth. Below the crust is the mantle, about 2,900 km of hot rock that can slowly flow.
At the centre is the core: a liquid outer core and a solid inner core, made of iron and nickel. Open the cutaway, drawn to true scale. Notice how thin the crust looks.

steps.say: Every dot is an earthquake from this week. Seismometers around the world record the waves each one sends through the planet.
Two kinds of wave travel through the inside. P waves push and pull, and can cross both solids and liquids. S waves shake side to side, and cannot travel through liquid.
Turn on x-ray to see each quake at its real depth. The deepest reach about 700 km, inside plates sinking at subduction zones like this one in the western Pacific.
S waves cannot cross the outer core, because it is liquid: about 2,200 km of molten iron and nickel. The solid inner core below it is about 1,250 km thick.
In 1936 the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann noticed P waves arriving in the 'shadow zone', where none were expected. She explained them with a solid inner core.
Open the cutaway. Find where the S-wave speed drops to zero: that is the boundary between the mantle and the core, 2,891 km down in the PREM model.

quiz.q: Which waves cannot travel through liquid?
quiz.why: S waves, the side-to-side shear waves, cannot travel through liquid. P waves can cross solids and liquids.
src: EARTH Magazine: March 29, 1936, notes on Earth's inner core

quiz.q: Who explained P waves in the 'shadow zone' with a solid inner core, in 1936?
quiz.why: The Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann proposed the solid inner core in 1936.
src: EARTH Magazine: March 29, 1936, notes on Earth's inner core

quiz.q: The Earth's core is nearly twice as dense as the mantle.
quiz.why: The core is metal (an iron-nickel alloy), not stone, which makes it nearly twice as dense as the mantle.
src: USGS: Inside the Earth (This Dynamic Earth)

quiz.q: About how deep do the deepest earthquakes happen?
quiz.why: Inside plates sinking at subduction zones, earthquakes happen down to about 700 km.

adult.title: Reading the core from seismic waves

steps.say: This week's biggest earthquake, M{quake.mag} {quake.place}, began {quake.depth} km down. The travel times of waves from quakes like this, recorded worldwide, are the main evidence for everything below the deepest drill hole, at about 12 km.

In 1909 Andrija Mohorovičić showed that a thin crust sits on the mantle. The USGS gives the crust about 5 km under the oceans and about 30 km on average under the continents, up to 100 km under big mountain ranges.
X-ray on: quakes at their real depth (drawn 25 times deeper). They stop at about 700 km, but the mantle goes on to about 2,900 km. Why they stop there is a question worth asking.

S waves cannot cross liquid; P waves can. In the PREM model the S-wave speed falls to zero at 2,891 km and P waves slow from 13.7 to 8.1 km/s: a liquid outer core. Inge Lehmann's 1936 reading of P waves arriving in the shadow zone added a solid inner core.
Open Inside the Earth and switch to Compare. PREM, IASP91 and ak135 are reference models fitted to travel times, not samples. They put the core-mantle boundary at 2,891, 2,889 and 2,891.5 km.

What the data can't show directly: the composition of the deep layers is inferred from wave speeds, density and high-pressure laboratory experiments. Whether there is an innermost inner core, and how the inner core turns, are still debated; the panel's cards give both sides with their papers.

quiz.q: In PREM the S-wave speed is zero from 2,891 to 5,149.5 km depth. What does that tell you?
quiz.why: S waves cannot travel through liquid, so a zero S-wave speed marks the liquid outer core.
src: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), Preliminary reference Earth model

quiz.q: Reference models like PREM are built from samples drilled out of the deep Earth.
quiz.why: They are fitted to the travel times of seismic waves recorded around the world (and other observations), not to samples.
src: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), Preliminary reference Earth model

A change in Earth's magnetic field

quiz.q: How thick is the liquid outer core, according to the USGS?
quiz.why: The USGS: a 2,200 km-thick liquid outer core and a 1,250 km-thick solid inner core.

The space station goes all the way around the Earth in about an hour and a half. That's so fast that the astronauts see 16 sunrises every day!
Now let's visit our Moon. The Moon goes around the Earth. It doesn't make its own light: the Sun lights it up.

steps.say: The space station, live. It completes an orbit about every 90 minutes at about 28,000 km/h. Try the maths: how many orbits fit in 24 hours?
The Moon. Half of it is always lit by the Sun. Its phase is simply how much of that lit half faces us. The phases repeat about every 29.5 days.

Everything you see in the sky, you see late. The Moon by about 1.3 seconds, the Sun by about 8 minutes 20 seconds.

steps.say: The Moon globe, built from Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery. Its radius is about 1,740 km; the whole Moon is less than a third as wide as Earth.

Model it: the Sun lights one half of the Moon at all times. The phases (new, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full, waning gibbous, third quarter, waning crescent) are just how much of that lit half faces Earth.

Two different months: the Moon orbits Earth in about 27.3 days, but new Moon to new Moon takes about 29.5 days, because Earth is also moving around the Sun and the Moon has to catch up to the same Sun-Earth line.

Earth and Moon are tidally locked: the Moon spins once per orbit, so we only see one side. The far side is not dark; at new Moon it is in full sunlight. Here the whole globe is lit evenly; drag it round to see the far side, which we never see from Earth.

steps.say: The Moon globe uses Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter imagery and the IAU's official feature names. It is lit evenly here so you can see the whole surface: notice the dark maria and the bright, cratered highlands.

Phases are pure geometry: one hemisphere is always sunlit, and we see a changing share of it over a synodic month of about 29.5 days. It is not Earth's shadow. Moonlight itself is dim: only about one-tenth of the sunlight hitting the Moon is reflected. This is the real lighting for this moment.

The 'dark side' is a misnomer. The Moon is tidally locked, so the far side never faces Earth, but it gets the same sunlight; at new Moon it is fully lit. Small wobbles called libration let us glimpse a little past the edges.

The maria are impact basins filled with basaltic lava between about 4.2 and 1.2 billion years ago; the brighter highlands are older and densely cratered. NASA counts more than 40 impact basins on the Moon.

All six Apollo landings, 1969 to 1972, were near the equator on the near side, timed for shortly after local sunrise, when the surface was cool and long shadows showed the terrain. Apollo 11 touched down in the southwestern Sea of Tranquility on 20 July 1969; twelve astronauts in all walked on the Moon.

Tides, briefly: the Moon's gravity raises two bulges, so most shorelines get two highs and two lows a day; the Sun adds roughly half as much, giving bigger spring tides at new and full Moon. Tonight's Moon: {moon.name}, {moon.lit}% lit.

quiz.q: Which statement about the Moon's far side is accurate?
a: It receives sunlight like the near side; we just never face it
It is lit only during lunar eclipses
quiz.why: Calling it the 'dark side' is misleading: different parts are in sunlight at different times, and at new Moon the far side is fully lit.

quiz.q: Roughly what share of the sunlight hitting the Moon does it reflect?

quiz.q: Spring tides happen at new and full Moon, when the Sun and Moon line up with Earth.
quiz.why: NASA: spring tides always happen when the Moon is at the full or new phase.

quiz.q: How many people walked on the Moon during the Apollo program (1969 to 1972)?
quiz.why: Six landings, each with two astronauts on the surface: twelve in all.

steps.say: Light-time is a ruler, and also a delay. You see the Moon about 1.3 seconds late and the Sun about 8 minutes 20 seconds late.

Voyager 1, launched 5 September 1977, is now about {voyager.lh} light-hours ({voyager.au} AU) from Earth, computed from JPL ephemerides. NASA calculated it would reach one light-day, about 25.9 billion km, on 18 November 2026.

Andromeda is about 2.5 million light-years away: you see it as it was 2.5 million years ago. On the cosmic web, galaxies and dark matter trace filaments; maps like this are inferred, not seen directly.

The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, yet the observable universe is about 92 billion light-years across, a radius of about 46 billion. Why? Space kept expanding while the light travelled, so the most distant galaxies, whose light left them about 13.5 billion years ago, are now much farther than 13.5 billion light-years away.

steps.say: Weather is a specific event over a short time; climate is the average over 30 years or more. One record-cold week is weather. To see climate you need long records, so let's read four of them.
Record 1: CO2 at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, sampled at about 3,400 m. Latest monthly mean: {co2.ppm} ppm. Same month last year: {co2.yago}. ppm means parts per million: 400 ppm is 0.000400 of the dry air.
Record 2: NOAA's global surface temperature. Its latest monthly ranking: {temp.when} ranks {temp.rank} warmest in {temp.n} years of records, compared with the 20th-century average.

Record 3: Arctic sea ice extent from satellites that sense microwaves, which pass through clouds and darkness. Today: {ice.ext} million km², against a 1979–2025 average of {ice.avg} for this date. The yearly maximum usually comes in March, the minimum in September.

Record 4: land ice. GRACE (2002–2017) and GRACE-FO (since 2018) are pairs of satellites about 220 km apart. Extra mass below pulls the lead satellite first, changing the gap. NASA reports Greenland losing about 265 billion metric tons a year since 2002.
Antarctica: about 135 billion metric tons a year since 2002, by the same method. Because this ice is on land, its meltwater adds to the ocean. Compare the colours here with Greenland's.

steps.say: A useful rule from NOAA: weather is a specific event over a short time; climate is average conditions over 30 years or more. Single days, storms or seasons are weather. Each record below is a long series from one agency, with its own method and blind spots.

CO2 at Mauna Loa: latest monthly mean {co2.ppm} ppm, against {co2.yago} in the same month a year earlier. The series began in March 1958 (C. David Keeling, Scripps). Its limits: one high-altitude site in the northern subtropics, a seasonal cycle driven mostly by land plants, and recent values marked preliminary until reference gases are recalibrated.

Global temperature: NOAA ranks {temp.when} {temp.rank} warmest in {temp.n} years, measured as an anomaly against the 20th-century average. A ranking hides how close the gaps are: NOAA reported July 2026 as tying 2024, and September 2026 as 0.07 °C short of 2023's record.

Arctic sea ice extent today: {ice.ext} million km², against a 1979–2025 same-date average of {ice.avg}. Extent is a threshold measure (cells at least 15% ice), not volume or thickness. NSIDC notes thin new ice is underestimated, the edge can be off by 25 to 50 km, and open water can exist inside 'ice-covered' cells.

Land ice by gravity: GRACE and GRACE-FO track the distance between twin satellites about 220 km apart to build monthly gravity maps. NASA gives Greenland about 265 billion metric tons lost per year since 2002. Limits: there is a gap from mid-2017 to mid-2018 between missions, data arrive up to two months late, and the method sees mass change, not which glacier caused it.

Antarctica: about 135 billion metric tons a year since 2002. The two ice sheets hold about two-thirds of Earth's fresh water, and NASA attributes about one-third of global average sea level rise since 1993 to their meltwater. Look at where on the continent the change is concentrated.

quiz.q: Arctic sea ice extent tells you how thick the ice is.
quiz.why: Extent counts area of cells with at least 15% ice; it says nothing about thickness, and thin new ice is underestimated.

steps.say: This layer shows six travellers: monarch butterflies, humpback whales, gray whales, Arctic terns, ruby-throated hummingbirds and barn swallows. Each line joins where people reported seeing them, month by month.

Why travel so far? Mostly for three reasons: food, a good place to have babies, and escaping the cold. Monarchs cannot survive the cold northern winter, so eastern monarchs fly up to 3,000 miles to mountain forests in Mexico.
Right now the monarchs' line ends in {mig.month}, centred near latitude {mig.lat}, which is {mig.dir} of the month before.

Important: these lines show where PEOPLE looked and shared sightings on iNaturalist, not one tagged animal. If lots of people go whale watching in one bay, the line can move there even if the whales did not.
Gray whales feed in the cold Bering and Chukchi seas in summer, then swim down to warm lagoons in Baja California, Mexico, to have calves. That is about 10,000 miles (about 16,000 km) round trip.
The Arctic tern beats them all. Tracked terns flew from Greenland to the Weddell Sea by Antarctica and back: more than 70,000 km (over 43,000 miles) in a year.

g68.title: Migration as a response to resources

steps.say: Six populations, each drawn as a line joining the monthly centre of iNaturalist sightings over the past 12 months. Watch which ones swing north-south with the seasons.

Migration follows resources. Humpback whales spend warm months feeding in cold, food-rich high-latitude waters, building fat, then move to shallow, warm tropical waters to calve. Some swim from Alaska to Hawaii, about 3,000 miles, in as few as 28 days.

Monarchs need two very different places: milkweed in summer (the only food their caterpillars eat) and cool, sheltered oyamel fir forests in Mexico in winter, at 2,400 to 3,600 metres. It takes 3 to 4 generations to get back north.
Live data: the monarch centre for {mig.month} sits near latitude {mig.lat}, {mig.dir} of the previous month. Is that the direction you'd predict for this time of year?
Remember the blind spot: this is a centre of where people reported sightings. More observers in cities, by roads, or on holiday can pull the centre without any animal moving.

Birds too. Ruby-throated hummingbirds leave eastern North America to winter from Mexico to Costa Rica or Panama; many UK barn swallows winter in South Africa, chasing flying insects. Arctic terns go pole to pole.

adult.title: Sightings versus tracks: reading migration data

steps.say: The Seasonal movement layer: for six populations, a line joining the monthly centre of iNaturalist community sightings over the past 12 months. It is a summary of observations, not a track.

Live: the eastern monarch centre for {mig.month} is near latitude {mig.lat}, {mig.dir} of the month before. Eastern monarchs spend October to late March in 11 to 12 mountain areas in the Mexican states of Mexico and Michoacán, in oyamel fir forest at 2,400 to 3,600 m. Overwintering adults in reproductive diapause can live six to nine months; breeding adults, two to five weeks.

The bias problem. Research Grade on iNaturalist means a dated, georeferenced, photo- or sound-backed wild observation with community agreement on the species. It does not mean even sampling. A British Columbia study found distance to roads was the strongest landscape factor explaining where observations are made. A centre computed from such data blends animal movement with human effort, holidays, and access, and it is presence-only: no record does not mean no animal.

The North Pacific: eastern North Pacific gray whales feed mainly in the northern Bering and Chukchi seas and winter off Baja California, about 10,000 miles round trip and in some cases upwards of 14,000, one of the longest annual migrations of any mammal. Humpbacks link Alaska with Hawaii and Mexico. Coastal whale-watching hot spots can dominate their sightings.

Real tracking looks different. In a 2010 PNAS study, 11 Arctic terns carried 1.4 g geolocators: they revealed a previously unknown stopover in the North Atlantic and more than 80,000 km a year for some birds. Movebank, hosted by the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior, archives billions of tag locations; BirdCast (Cornell Lab, UMass Amherst, Oregon State) maps night migration from weather radar and forecasts it three days ahead.

g68.title: Who made this, when, and why?

steps.say: Historians ask three questions of any source: who made it, when, and why? Let's try them on two old almanacs.
1846: a list of banks marked 'fraud'. In the 1840s, many private banks printed their own paper money, and some notes became worthless. The almanac warned its readers.

1923: 'Colder, with probable snow flurries. Time to be stocking up…' Ask why: every month on this page names a Colgate product. It is an advertisement dressed up as a forecast; almanacs sold pages to advertisers.

Check old claims against new evidence. In 1846 the almanac said Russia was the only country in Europe still on the old calendar. Russia switched in 1918, but Greece also kept the old calendar until 1923: the almanac was not quite right even then.

quiz.q: The 1846 almanac lists banks marked 'fraud'. What does that tell you about money then?
a: Banks printed their own notes, and some were not worth their full value
The U.S. government printed all paper money
quiz.why: Before the Civil War, U.S. paper money was mostly notes issued by state-chartered banks, often accepted only at a discount. The almanac's list warned readers which notes to refuse.

steps.say: Every source on this site comes with three things: who published it, how it was checked, and its blind spot. Try that habit on two almanacs.
Context: a 1846 list of 'uncurrent' and fraudulent banks only makes sense in a world where private banks issued their own notes.
Purpose: in 1923 an advertiser wrote its ad to look like an almanac forecast. A source can be genuine and still be selling something.
Corroboration: the 1923 almanac's figure for the nearest star (4.4 years for light) was close to today's for Alpha Centauri, but Proxima Centauri, slightly nearer, had been found in 1915.
